subproblems.title: Gram matrix of a linear map: symmetric, positive semidefinite, with trace |D|^2
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers n, l and every continuous linear map D : R^n -> R^l (D : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ), let e_a := EuclideanSpace.single a 1 (a in Fin n) be the standard basis of R^n and let G be the real n x n matrix G_ab := <D e_a, D e_b> (Matrix.of fun a b => inner ℝ (D e_a) (D e_b)). Then (i) G is symmetric, G^T = G (Matrix.IsSymm G); (ii) for every x : Fin n -> R the quadratic form x . (G x) = sum_a x_a sum_b G_ab x_b (dotProduct x (Matrix.mulVec G x)) is >= 0; (iii) trace G = sum_a G_aa equals hsNormSq D = sum_a |D e_a|^2.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (D : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ), Matrix.IsSymm (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin n => inner ℝ (D (EuclideanSpace.single a (1 : ℝ))) (D (EuclideanSpace.single b (1 : ℝ)))) ∧ (∀ x : Fin n → ℝ, 0 ≤ dotProduct x (Matrix.mulVec (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin n => inner ℝ (D (EuclideanSpace.single a (1 : ℝ))) (D (EuclideanSpace.single b (1 : ℝ)))) x)) ∧ Matrix.trace (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin n => inner ℝ (D (EuclideanSpace.single a (1 : ℝ))) (D (EuclideanSpace.single b (1 : ℝ)))) = hsNormSq D
subproblems.natural_proof:
Context. This child is the Gram-matrix half of steps 1, 2 and 6 of the parent proof. It shows that G = (<D e_a, D e_b>) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, which are the hypotheses of the sibling gwe_gjb_det_one_add_bounds. It also shows trace G = hsNormSq D, which lets the parent rewrite exp(trace G) as exp(hsNormSq D).

Notation.
- e_a := EuclideanSpace.single a 1 is the a-th standard basis vector of R^n = EuclideanSpace R (Fin n).
- v_a := D e_a, a vector in R^l.
- G := Matrix.of (fun a b => <v_a, v_b>), so G_ab = <v_a, v_b> (Matrix.of_apply).
- For x, y : Fin n -> R, dotProduct x y = sum_i x_i y_i, and (Matrix.mulVec G x)_a = sum_b G_ab x_b. Over R there is no conjugation.
- The inner product on R^l = EuclideanSpace R (Fin l) is the real Euclidean one. It is bilinear and symmetric, and <w, w> = ||w||^2 >= 0.

1. Symmetry (i). Matrix.IsSymm G means G^T = G. By matrix extensionality it suffices to show (G^T)_ab = G_ab for all a, b. Indeed (G^T)_ab = G_ba = <v_b, v_a> = <v_a, v_b> = G_ab, by symmetry of the real inner product (real_inner_comm).
2. Expanding the quadratic form (ii). Fix x : Fin n -> R. By the definitions of dotProduct and mulVec, after distributing x_a over the inner sum,
   x . (G x) = sum_a x_a (sum_b <v_a, v_b> x_b) = sum_a sum_b x_a x_b <v_a, v_b>.
3. Let w := sum_a x_a • v_a in R^l. By bilinearity of the real inner product (sum_inner, inner_sum, inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right; conjugation is trivial over R),
   <w, w> = sum_a sum_b x_a x_b <v_a, v_b>.
   If the expansion yields <v_b, v_a> in the (a, b) summand, rewrite it to <v_a, v_b> with real_inner_comm. The scalar factors then agree by commutativity of multiplication.
4. By steps 2 and 3, x . (G x) = <w, w> >= 0 (real_inner_self_nonneg).
5. Trace (iii). Matrix.trace G is the sum of the diagonal entries, so
   trace G = sum_a G_aa = sum_a <v_a, v_a> = sum_a ||D e_a||^2 (real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq).
   By definition this is hsNormSq D = sum_{i : Fin n} ||D (EuclideanSpace.single i 1)||^2.
6. Case n = 0. All sums are empty and G is the empty matrix. So (i) holds by extensionality over the empty index type, the form in (ii) is 0 >= 0, and trace G = 0 = hsNormSq D. Steps 1-5 cover this case verbatim. QED

Lean notes. Checked against the pinned toolchain, using only the contract's imports.
- (i): ext i j; simp only [Matrix.transpose_apply, Matrix.of_apply]; exact real_inner_comm _ _.
- (ii): state the identity of steps 2-3 as a `have`. Prove it by simp only [dotProduct, Matrix.mulVec, Matrix.of_apply, sum_inner, inner_sum, inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right, Finset.mul_sum], then Finset.sum_congr twice, conj_trivial, rw [real_inner_comm (D (EuclideanSpace.single a (1 : ℝ)))] and ring. Finish with real_inner_self_nonneg.
- (iii): simp only [Matrix.trace, Matrix.diag, Matrix.of_apply, hsNormSq, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq].
proof_key_steps: G^T = G entrywise, by symmetry of the real inner product.
x . (G x) = sum_a sum_b x_a x_b <D e_a, D e_b> = <w, w> with w = sum_a x_a D e_a, by bilinearity.
<w, w> >= 0, so G is positive semidefinite.
trace G = sum_a <D e_a, D e_a> = sum_a ||D e_a||^2 = hsNormSq D.

subproblems.title: Determinant bounds 1 <= det(I + G) <= exp(trace G) for a symmetric positive semidefinite real matrix G
subproblems.statement: For every natural number n and every real n x n matrix G (G : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) assume two things: G is symmetric, G^T = G (Matrix.IsSymm G); and G is positive semidefinite, x . (G x) = sum_a x_a sum_b G_ab x_b >= 0 for every x : Fin n -> R (0 <= dotProduct x (Matrix.mulVec G x)). Let I be the n x n identity matrix and I + G the entrywise sum. Then 1 <= det(I + G) and det(I + G) <= exp(trace G).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ), Matrix.IsSymm G → (∀ x : Fin n → ℝ, 0 ≤ dotProduct x (Matrix.mulVec G x)) → 1 ≤ Matrix.det ((1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) + G) ∧ Matrix.det ((1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) + G) ≤ Real.exp (Matrix.trace G)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Context. This child is steps 1-7 of the parent proof in matrix form. The parent applies it to the Gram matrix G = (<D e_a, D e_b>) of D. The sibling gwe_gjb_gram_symm_psd_trace supplies the symmetry and positive semidefiniteness of G and trace G = hsNormSq D. Then 1 <= det(I + G) gives part (i) after taking square roots, and det(I + G) <= exp(trace G) = exp(hsNormSq D) is step 7.

Notation.
- A := I + G, a real n x n matrix indexed by Fin n.
- For x, y : Fin n -> R, x . y := dotProduct x y = sum_i x_i y_i.
- A x := Matrix.mulVec A x, with (A x)_i = sum_j A_ij x_j.
- The symmetry hypothesis is essential. G = [[0, 1], [-1, 0]] has x . (G x) = 0 for every x, but det(I + G) = 2 > 1 = exp(trace G).

1. A is symmetric, hence Hermitian. A^T = I^T + G^T = I + G = A (transpose_add, transpose_one and the hypothesis G^T = G). Over R the star operation is trivial, so the conjugate transpose of A equals A^T (Matrix.conjTranspose_eq_transpose_of_trivial). Hence A^H = A, i.e. A is Hermitian (Matrix.IsHermitian A).
2. Quadratic form of A. For every x : Fin n -> R we have A x = x + G x (Matrix.add_mulVec, Matrix.one_mulVec). So, by dotProduct_add and the hypothesis,
   x . (A x) = x . x + x . (G x) >= x . x.
3. Spectral theorem. A is Hermitian, so the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices (Mathlib.Analysis.Matrix.Spectrum) applies. It gives real numbers lambda_i := hA.eigenvalues i (i in Fin n) and an orthonormal basis u_i := hA.eigenvectorBasis i of EuclideanSpace R (Fin n), with A u_i = lambda_i u_i. It also gives lambda_i = re(star u_i . (A u_i)) (Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues_eq). Over R, re is the identity and star u_i = u_i, so lambda_i = u_i . (A u_i).
4. Every eigenvalue is at least 1. The basis is orthonormal, so ||u_i|| = 1. Also ||u_i||^2 = sum_j (u_i)_j^2 = u_i . u_i (EuclideanSpace.norm_sq_eq), so u_i . u_i = 1. By steps 2 and 3,
   lambda_i = u_i . (A u_i) = u_i . u_i + u_i . (G u_i) >= 1.
   In particular every lambda_i > 0.
5. Determinant and trace via eigenvalues. det A = prod_i lambda_i (Matrix.IsHermitian.det_eq_prod_eigenvalues) and trace A = sum_i lambda_i (Matrix.IsHermitian.trace_eq_sum_eigenvalues). Over R the coercions R -> R in these formulas are the identity.
6. Lower bound. Every factor lambda_i is >= 1, so det A = prod_i lambda_i >= 1, since a finite product of factors >= 1 is >= 1 (Finset.one_le_prod₀). For n = 0 the product is empty and equals 1.
7. Trace of A. trace A = trace I + trace G = n + trace G (Matrix.trace_add, Matrix.trace_one, card (Fin n) = n).
8. Upper bound. For each i, lambda_i = (lambda_i - 1) + 1 <= exp(lambda_i - 1) (Real.add_one_le_exp), and lambda_i >= 0 by step 4. All factors are nonnegative, so the products compare factor by factor (Finset.prod_le_prod₀):
   det A = prod_i lambda_i <= prod_i exp(lambda_i - 1) = exp(sum_i (lambda_i - 1)) = exp(trace A - n) = exp(trace G).
   The first equality is Real.exp_sum. The second uses sum_i (lambda_i - 1) = sum_i lambda_i - n = trace A - n (step 5). The third is step 7.
9. Conclusion. Since A is literally (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R) + G, steps 6 and 8 are the two claimed inequalities.
10. Case n = 0. All products are empty and all sums vanish: det A = 1 and trace G = 0. So the claims read 1 <= 1 and 1 <= exp 0 = 1, and steps 6 and 8 cover this case verbatim. QED

subproblems.title: Scalar bound exp(s/2) <= 1 + (e^{T/2}/2) s for 0 <= s <= T
subproblems.statement: For all real numbers s and T with 0 <= s and s <= T: exp(s/2) <= 1 + (exp(T/2)/2) * s.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (s T : ℝ), 0 ≤ s → s ≤ T → Real.exp (s / 2) ≤ 1 + Real.exp (T / 2) / 2 * s
subproblems.natural_proof:
Context. This child is steps 10-11 of the parent proof. The parent first bounds J(D) = sqrt(det(I + G)) <= sqrt(exp(hsNormSq D)) = exp(hsNormSq D / 2). It then applies this child with s = hsNormSq D and T = n; here 0 <= s, and s <= n when ||D|| <= 1.

1. Put t := s/2. From 0 <= s <= T we get 0 <= t and t <= T/2.
2. Real.add_one_le_exp at -t gives -t + 1 <= exp(-t), i.e. 1 - t <= exp(-t).
3. Multiply step 2 by exp t > 0:
   (1 - t) exp t <= exp(-t) exp t = exp(-t + t) = exp 0 = 1 (Real.exp_add, Real.exp_zero).
   Rearranged: exp t <= 1 + t exp t.
4. exp is monotone and t <= T/2, so exp t <= exp(T/2) (Real.exp_le_exp). Multiplying by t >= 0 gives t exp t <= t exp(T/2).
5. By steps 3 and 4,
   exp(s/2) = exp t <= 1 + t exp(T/2) = 1 + (s/2) exp(T/2) = 1 + (exp(T/2)/2) s. QED

Lean note. Checked against the pinned toolchain: with h2 : (1 - s / 2) * Real.exp (s / 2) ≤ 1 and h4 : s / 2 * Real.exp (s / 2) ≤ s / 2 * Real.exp (T / 2) in context, nlinarith [h2, h4] closes the goal.
proof_key_steps: 1 - t <= exp(-t) for t = s/2 (add_one_le_exp at -t).
Multiplying by exp t > 0 gives exp t <= 1 + t exp t.
t <= T/2 and t >= 0 give t exp t <= t exp(T/2), so exp(s/2) <= 1 + (exp(T/2)/2) s.

subproblems.title: Hilbert-Schmidt norm: continuity and comparison with the operator norm
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers m, k: the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm hsNormSq(A) = sum over i < m of |A e_i|^2 (e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1, the standard basis of R^m) is a continuous function of A on the space of continuous linear maps R^m -> R^k with the operator-norm topology; and for every such A: 0 <= hsNormSq(A), hsNormSq(A) <= m ||A||^2 where ||A|| is the operator norm, and |A v|^2 <= hsNormSq(A) |v|^2 for every v in R^m.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m k : ℕ), Continuous (fun A : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k => hsNormSq A) ∧ ∀ A : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k, 0 ≤ hsNormSq A ∧ hsNormSq A ≤ m * ‖A‖ ^ 2 ∧ ∀ v : Rn m, ‖A v‖ ^ 2 ≤ hsNormSq A * ‖v‖ ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Context. Here this child supplies step 9 of the parent proof. Its conjuncts 0 <= hsNormSq A and hsNormSq A <= m ||A||^2, with A = D and m = n, give 0 <= |D|^2 <= n ||D||^2. When ||D|| <= 1 we have 0 <= ||D|| <= 1, so ||D||^2 <= 1 and n ||D||^2 <= n; hence 0 <= |D|^2 <= n. This child is the comparator-accepted declaration of DAG node root.lipschitz_graph_corollary-a1.hole_estimate-a1.hs_norm_bounds-a1 (candidate commit 7372f81c6640dd17bd99bd3c9bbe79675f27d126). It is reused with its identical frozen Lean type, title, statement and empty dependency list. The proof below is its accepted proof.

Notation. e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 for i in Fin m; these vectors form the standard orthonormal basis of R^m, so |e_i| = 1. For v in R^m, v_i denotes its i-th coordinate. By definition hsNormSq(A) = sum over i < m of |A e_i|^2. ||A|| is the operator norm of A : R^m ->L R^k.

1. Continuity. Fix i. The evaluation map A -> A e_i is linear in A and satisfies |A e_i - B e_i| = |(A - B) e_i| <= ||A - B|| |e_i| = ||A - B||, so it is continuous for the operator-norm topology. Composing with the continuous maps w -> |w| and t -> t^2 gives a continuous real function A -> |A e_i|^2. A finite sum of continuous real functions is continuous, so A -> sum_i |A e_i|^2 = hsNormSq(A) is continuous.
2. Nonnegativity. Every summand |A e_i|^2 is >= 0, hence hsNormSq(A) >= 0.
3. Upper bound by the operator norm. For each i, 0 <= |A e_i| <= ||A|| |e_i| = ||A||, so |A e_i|^2 <= ||A||^2. Summing over the m indices gives hsNormSq(A) <= sum_{i<m} ||A||^2 = m ||A||^2.
4. Coordinates. Every v in R^m satisfies v = sum_i v_i e_i, because the j-th coordinate of the right side is sum_i v_i delta_{ij} = v_j. For the Euclidean norm, |v|^2 = sum_i v_i^2 = sum_i |v_i|^2.
5. Bound on |A v|. By linearity of A and step 4, A v = sum_i v_i (A e_i). The triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm give |A v| <= sum_i |v_i (A e_i)| = sum_i |v_i| |A e_i|.
6. Cauchy-Schwarz. For finite sums of real numbers, (sum_i a_i b_i)^2 <= (sum_i a_i^2)(sum_i b_i^2). With a_i = |v_i| and b_i = |A e_i| and step 4, (sum_i |v_i| |A e_i|)^2 <= (sum_i |v_i|^2)(sum_i |A e_i|^2) = |v|^2 hsNormSq(A).
7. Conclusion. Since 0 <= |A v| <= sum_i |v_i| |A e_i| (step 5), squaring preserves the inequality, and step 6 gives |A v|^2 <= (sum_i |v_i| |A e_i|)^2 <= hsNormSq(A) |v|^2. If m = 0, all sums are empty and v = 0, so each assertion reads 0 <= 0 and the steps above apply verbatim. QED
proof_key_steps: Continuity: each evaluation A -> A e_i is continuous linear, and hsNormSq is a finite sum of squared norms of such maps.
Nonnegativity: hsNormSq A is a sum of squares.
|A e_i| <= ||A|| |e_i| = ||A||; summing over i < m gives hsNormSq A <= m ||A||^2.
Expand v = sum_i v_i e_i; linearity and the triangle inequality give |A v| <= sum_i |v_i| |A e_i|.
Cauchy-Schwarz gives (sum_i |v_i| |A e_i|)^2 <= |v|^2 hsNormSq A; squaring the nonnegative bound gives |A v|^2 <= hsNormSq A |v|^2.
